Dangling-reference repairs:

1. "The term is derived from the same Greek word …": the referring words are "The term". Repair: name span. I appended "pragmatism", taken from the segment's opening sentence ("what pragmatism means").
2. "In an article entitled 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear,' in the 'Popular Science Monthly' for January of that year[^1] Mr. Peirce, after pointing out …": the referring words are "that year". The words also carry the source's footnote marker. Repair: cut. The trimmed citation only points (it is bibliographic) and carries no argument content. The trace starts at "Mr. Peirce".
3. "I found a few years ago that Ostwald … had been making perfectly distinct use of the principle of pragmatism …": the referring words are "I found a few years ago that". Repair: first-person cut. It is the author's framing of how he knows the fact.
4. "\"All realities influence our practice,\" he wrote me, \"and that influence is their meaning for us.": the referring word is "me". Repair: first-person cut, leaving a mid-sentence cut joined with "{, }". "he" is kept because the preceding statement supplies its referent, Ostwald.
5. "I am accustomed to put questions to my classes …" and "If I can find nothing that would become different …": these "I"/"my" belong to Ostwald, inside his quoted speech, not to the author. Their referent is supplied by "he wrote" (Ostwald) and the open quotation, so I left them unrepaired.

"we"/"you" judged generic and left unrepaired:

- "our beliefs", "we need only determine", "for us its sole significance", "our thoughts", "we are to expect", "we must prepare", "for us the whole of our conception", "there is for us none": all mean people in general.
- "our words 'practice' and 'practical'": speakers of English generally.
- "one must get accustomed".
- "the moment you subject them": addressed to the reader.
- "to you and me, at definite instants of our life": "you and me" here means anyone, not the author specifically.
- "in our time": the present age generally.

Statements dropped:

- "I believe in that destiny, and I hope I may end by inspiring you with my belief." Dropped by selection: it states the author's stance and hope, not a premise or conclusion. Keeping it would have needed the author name span.
- Dropped by selection as history or story:
  - "A glance at the history of the idea …" (transition).
  - "It lay entirely unnoticed by anyone for twenty years, until I … brought it forward again …"
  - "By that date (1898) the times seemed ripe …"
  - "On all hands we find the 'pragmatic movement' spoken of …"
- Dropped as an illustration of the principle, not a proposition: Ostwald's tautomerous-bodies example and his quoted comment on that quarrel ("Ostwald in a published lecture gives this example …" through the brownie/elf quote).

No asides.
